summary.text: The Holocaust, known in Hebrew as the Shoah, was the genocide of European Jews during World War II.
From 1941 to 1945, Nazi Germany and its collaborators systematically murdered around six million Jews, approximately two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population.
The murders were committed mainly through mass shootings across Eastern Europe and poison gas chambers in extermination camps in occupied Poland.

facts.label: Hebrew name
facts.value: Shoah, a word that refers only to Jewish victims

facts.label: Victims
facts.value: Around six million Jews, two-thirds of Europe's Jews

facts.label: Final Solution
facts.value: Implemented by early 1942, after the Wannsee Conference

items.prompt: A writer in the 1800s uses the word holocaust in everyday English. What would a reader have understood?

options.label: The Nazi murder of European Jews
Destruction or sacrifice by fire, or figuratively a massacre
Any famine that struck a whole country
A ceremony of remembrance for the dead

items.explain: The word was an ordinary English word for centuries meaning destruction or sacrifice by fire, or figuratively massacre, and only became the name for the Nazi extermination from the 1950s.

items.prompt: Why might a speaker choose the word Shoah rather than Holocaust?

options.label: Shoah covers all groups the Nazis persecuted
Holocaust is a word that never covers Jews
Shoah means a single event in 1942
Shoah refers exclusively to Jewish victims

items.explain: Holocaust is sometimes used to include other persecuted groups, while Shoah exclusively refers to Jewish victims.

items.prompt: After the June 1941 invasion of the Soviet Union, the Nazis first target certain Jews. How did the killing then change?

options.label: It quickly escalated to murdering Jewish women and children
It shifted to forced emigration of Jewish families
It paused while ghettos were being built
It ended once Red Army prisoners were killed

items.explain: The Nazis first targeted Jewish Red Army POWs and male civilians, but quickly escalated to women and children.

items.prompt: In the 1930s the Nazi regime passed anti-Jewish laws and encouraged violence. What was this meant to achieve?

options.label: To move German Jews into ghettos in Poland
To prepare an exchange for German prisoners
To force all German Jews to leave the country
To win Jewish support for the new regime

items.explain: The measures were meant to force all German Jews to emigrate, regardless of means.

items.prompt: The killing was at its most intense from March 1942 to November 1943. Did the mass murders stop then?

options.label: Yes, they stopped once Operation Reinhard ended
No, they continued until the end of the war in 1945
Yes, they stopped after the Wannsee Conference
No, they continued until the 1950s

items.explain: Most victims died in 1942, but the mass murders continued until the end of the war in 1945.

items.prompt: Many Germans after 1918 wanted an explanation for losing the war. Which explanation from the military is described as untrue?

options.label: That socialists and Jews betrayed Germany, which was not beaten in battle
That Germany lost because it simply ran out of men to fight
That Germany was never defeated and had really won the war
That Germany lost because its own generals made poor choices

items.explain: The military promoted the untrue idea that Germany had been stabbed in the back by socialists and Jews rather than defeated on the battlefield.
